title: Unordered Lists 🔘
description: Create bulleted lists with `<ul>` and `<li>`, and nest them for complex outlines.

slides.title: Why Lists? 📋
slides.content:
# Organise Items Naturally

Lists are everywhere on the web: navigation menus, recipe ingredients, to‑do items, feature summaries. HTML gives us dedicated tags:
- **Unordered list** (`<ul>`) – bullet points.
- **Ordered list** (`<ol>`) – numbered steps.
- **Description list** (`<dl>`) – terms and definitions.

Using the right list tag makes your content more meaningful and accessible.

slides.title: The `<ul>` and `<li>` Duo 🤝
slides.content:
# Bullet Points in Code `
    ` stands for **unordered list**. Each item inside is wrapped in a `
  • ` (list item). ```html
    • Apples
    • Bananas
    • Cherries
    ``` Browsers automatically add bullet points. The list is a block element; items are block too, but you can change that with CSS.

quizData.question: Which tag directly wraps each item in an unordered list?
quizData.explanation: <li> (list item) is used for each item inside both <ul> and <ol> lists.

slides.title: Nesting Lists 🪆
slides.content:
# Lists Inside Lists You can put a `
    ` (or `
      `) inside an `
    1. ` to create sub‑levels. This is perfect for outlines or menu dropdowns. ```html
      • Fruits
        • Apples
        • Oranges
      • Vegetables
      ``` The inner `
        ` must be completely inside the parent `
      • ` (before its closing tag).

quizData.question: An inner list should be placed directly inside the outer `<ul>`, not inside an `<li>`.
quizData.explanation: Nested lists must be inside an `<li>` element. The `<ul>` cannot be a direct child of another `<ul>` without an intervening `<li>`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Don't Use Lists for Everything

Use lists only when the content is a collection of items. For purely visual grouping, a `<div>` may be better. Semantics first!
